slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
The mechanism is the one from the first video of this module: a rebase copies.
Your colleague's clone, her own copy of the repository, still holds the originals, with her own work on top.
The second half of the video is about your own mistakes.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.headline: Section 9.16, in one sentence
slides.body: A rebase destroys nothing: the old tip is named by ORIG_HEAD until another command overwrites that ref, and by the reflog of the branch for weeks.

slides.direction: The three handles.
rows: While the rebase is in progress
Discards resolution work done so far
Rewritten by the next git reset, git merge, git rebase or git am
One entry per rebase, so count in the listing; a deleted branch has no reflog

items: Following the git pull hint after your own rebase was rejected on push. Root cause: the server still has the originals; a pull merges them next to your copies or replaces your copies with them.
Merging after a "(forced update)" on a branch you have built on. Root cause: commits are identified by ID, so the copies and the originals are different commits, and a merge keeps both lines.
Pushing that merge. Root cause: it makes the removed commits reachable on the server again, which undoes a rewrite whose purpose was to remove something.
Relying on ORIG_HEAD hours after a rebase. Root cause: it is one slot, rewritten by the next reset, merge, rebase or git am.
Moving the real branch before creating a rescue ref. Root cause: until a ref points at the recovered commits, they are reachable only through reflog entries that further commands keep pushing down.

slides.body: Today you played both sides of a duplicated history, and you recovered a branch from its reflog.

beats.text: The CTO is looking at a branch.
beats.tele: The CTO is looking at a branch.

beats.text: "Add document loader" appears in it twice, with two different IDs. So does "Add text cleaner". There's a merge commit on top, a commit with two parents, that nobody remembers wanting.
beats.tele: "Add document loader" appears in it twice, with two different IDs. So does "Add text cleaner". There's a merge commit on top, a commit with two parents, that nobody remembers wanting.

beats.text: Two engineers were involved. One rebased the branch and force-pushed it, with a lease, exactly as the documentation recommends. The other fetched, read what git status suggested, and followed the suggestion. Each did something reasonable. Together they produced a history in which every change is recorded twice.
beats.tele: Two engineers were involved. One rebased the branch and force-pushed it, with a lease, exactly as the documentation recommends. The other fetched, read what `git status` suggested, and followed the suggestion. Each did something reasonable. Together they produced a history in which every change is recorded twice.

beats.text: You're going to play both roles, watch the duplication happen, and then repair it. After that you break a branch on your own, lose the obvious way back, and recover it anyway. Which reasonable step did the damage? Hold your guess.
